name: service-locator
intent: Provide one registry from which a component can obtain its collaborators at run time by type, interface or name, so that code with no usable injection point can still receive configured services - at the price of making its dependency graph invisible to the compiler.
problem: Some objects are created by code you do not own: framework callbacks, servlets and filters, pages and activities, plugin hosts, deserialized or reflection-built types. There is no constructor to hand collaborators to, so each such site either repeats the same lookup-and-cache code or reaches for a different global, and the wiring decision is spread over the code instead of sitting in one configuration step.
context: Long-lived applications that have (or can have) a single composition root, where a minority of call sites cannot be injected: types instantiated by a framework, plugin or extensibility points that must obtain host services, configuration-driven selection of an implementation by name, and libraries that must work with whatever container their host uses. It is also the mechanism a container itself exposes (JNDI, ServiceLoader, IServiceProvider, ApplicationContext, Koin's get) for code that sits outside the container's own construction path.
benefits: Reaches code that has no injection point: a framework-created object can resolve the one collaborator the framework cannot hand it, which keeps such code injectable in spirit instead of forcing a global per dependency.

Separates configuration from use: implementations, names and lifetimes are chosen once in the composition root, so a deployment change does not edit the constructors of every consumer (Fowler's core justification for both injection and lookup).

Late binding: the implementation can be selected from configuration, a registry key or the environment at startup - or swapped at run time - which suits plugins, feature-gated integrations and per-tenant variants.

Lets a library adapt to any host: resolving through an abstract locator (JVM ServiceLoader, Prism's IServiceLocator, a key-path container in Swift) lets a component obtain host services without binding itself to one container or one wiring style.
Economies of scale for genuinely expensive lookups: the J2EE form caches initial contexts and factory objects so that every client does not repeat the same naming-service round trip.

Gives otherwise untestable code a seam: a test can register a double for the duration of the test and remove it again, which is how framework-created objects are tested when their constructors cannot be called directly.
tradeoffs: Hidden dependencies: the constructor no longer says what the object needs, so dependencies must be found by searching the source for lookups (Fowler) and the object cannot be reasoned about - or constructed - without a populated registry.

Failures move from compile time to run time: a missing or mistyped key surfaces as NullInjectorError, NoSuchBeanDefinitionException, InvalidOperationException, KeyError or NameError on the path that first runs it (Seemann's central objection), and a partially configured deployment passes every build.

The locator becomes a coupling point of its own: every consumer depends on the locator's API, narrowing it to a role interface still requires seeing the locator, and a component shipped to another team may not know their locator at all (which is why Fowler prefers injection for reusable components).

Lifetime and scope rules hide behind the lookup: one key may return a cached singleton, a fresh instance or a request-scoped object, and resolving a shorter-lived service from a longer-lived locator silently captures it (the .NET captive-dependency case that scope validation exists to catch).
Ambient authority: whoever holds the locator can obtain every registered service, so module boundaries, least privilege and encapsulation are no longer expressed by types or visibility.

Diagnostics and refactoring weaken: no static reference connects a consumer to the resolved implementation, so find-usages, dead-code detection and dependency visualisation degrade, and registration-order or duplicate-registration mistakes (registration after first use, two modules registering the same key) appear only when that path executes.

participants.responsibility: Owns the key-to-provider mapping and returns an instance for a lookup, applying the lifetime rule recorded at registration (singleton, per-lookup, scoped) and failing in a defined way when the key is unknown.
The factory, instance or class registered under a key; it states how the service is created and how long the registry may keep it.
The object that cannot be handed its collaborators; it asks the locator for a service by key and uses the interface it gets back, without knowing the implementation.

The single place, run before clients by the application entry point, that fills the locator: implementation choices, names, lifetimes and configuration - and the only place that should know concrete types.
The abstraction the client depends on and that the lookup is keyed by; it keeps clients independent of implementations and gives the key a compile-time shape.

use_cases: Framework-instantiated types with no usable constructor: ASP.NET pages and middleware, Java servlets and filters, Android activities and workers, SwiftUI views - resolve the one dependency the framework cannot inject, inside the object's initialisation hook, and pass real dependencies on from there.

Configuration-driven implementation choice: the deployment names the renderer, payment provider or storage backend, and a registry resolves that name from the class path, installed distributions (Python entry points, JVM ServiceLoader) or a driver-style map (Go's database/sql).

Plugin and extension hosts: the application offers services such as logging, configuration and repositories to plugins it did not compile against, handing each plugin a narrow locator or role interface at registration time.

Libraries that must stay container-agnostic: a component resolves framework services through an abstract locator instead of forcing a container choice on its users (Prism's IServiceLocator, ServiceLoader on the JVM, key-path containers in Swift).

Legacy enterprise code where the platform is the naming service: JNDI lookups of data sources, connection factories and mail sessions, with the locator caching the initial context and the looked-up factories.
Test harnesses for objects that cannot be constructed directly: register a double under the key for the duration of the test, exercise the framework-created object, then remove the registration.

Dynamic module platforms where services appear and disappear at run time: in OSGi, a bundle looks a service up through BundleContext - getServiceReference selects among competing registrations by SERVICE_RANK and service id, getService honours the declared scope (singleton, per-bundle, prototype) - and the lookup can legitimately return null once the providing bundle stops, so the client must handle arrival and departure rather than assume a fixed graph.

PHP frameworks whose docs ship lookup as the escape hatch for code outside the injection path: Laravel resolves bindings with App::make(...) or the app() helper (the container implements PSR-11, so Psr\Container\ContainerInterface can itself be injected where a constructor is reachable), which is how facades and framework-created classes reach container bindings without a constructor.
avoid_when: The class is created by your own code: pass collaborators through the constructor (dependency injection) and delete the lookup - the compiler then checks the graph and the dependency is visible in the signature.

You are already inside a DI container: use constructor or property injection instead of asking the container for instances (Spring, ASP.NET Core, Angular, Koin and NestJS all document this explicitly), because mixing strategies hides the graph the container was there to make explicit.
The dependency is a value or a pure function with no configuration or lifecycle: pass it as a parameter or a field rather than routing it through a registry.
The object graph is small and static - a script, a CLI with three collaborators, one service: build it inline at the entry point; a registry buys indirection and runtime errors for nothing.
What you actually need is per-module wiring policy or interception: a composition root with explicit parameters, or a framework's injection pipeline, does that without a global lookup.
anti_patterns: Locator as an ambient god-object: a static container reachable from anywhere, used as a "virtual new operator" (Seemann's phrase), so what a component may use is unknowable and every test needs global setup.
Hiding dependencies to satisfy a purity rule: constructors take nothing and every collaborator is resolved inside methods, leaving types that cannot be constructed or asserted in isolation.
String-keyed lookups with no compile-time contract: renames and typos become runtime nulls, KeyErrors or NameErrors that no IDE can follow.
Rebuilding a locator on top of a framework that already provides one (a hand-rolled registry inside Spring, Angular or ASP.NET Core), producing two graphs, two lifetime policies and two truths.

Using the locator as a factory for objects with runtime arguments (per-request objects, entities built from a result set), which confuses identity and lifetime instead of using construction or a factory.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: configuration of services is separated from their use, and lookup is confined to the seam that cannot be injected.
Dependency inversion: the client depends on the service interface and a key, never on a concrete implementation.
Open/closed principle: new implementations are registered rather than wired into consumers, so consumers stay closed for modification.
Least knowledge, applied as the limit of the pattern: constructor injection is the default and lookup is the documented exception, because the pattern trades explicitness for reach.
Single responsibility: the composition root owns wiring while domain code owns behaviour - a locator reached from inside a domain object means both responsibilities collapsed.
best_practices: Confine lookups to the seams that genuinely lack an injection point (framework callbacks, plugin entry points, serialization hooks) and treat that site as a Humble Object: resolve once, then pass real dependencies on.

Key by the service interface or by a typed token, not by a free-form string; where a name is unavoidable (configuration, driver registration, JNDI), resolve it in one place and validate it at startup.

Record the lifetime explicitly at registration (singleton, per-lookup, scoped) and validate it - never resolve a shorter-lived service from a longer-lived locator, and switch on the container's scope validation where it exists.
Fail loudly and early: throw on unknown keys instead of returning null, and pre-flight the registry at startup so a missing binding fails before traffic arrives.

Keep registration single-threaded and duplicate-free (register before threads start, reject duplicate keys), and give tests an explicit way to build an isolated registry rather than mutating a global one.
Expose a role interface with only the lookups a module needs, so holding the locator does not imply authority over every service.
sources: Alur, Crupi & Malks, Core J2EE Patterns: Best Practices and Design Strategies (2001/2003) - Service Locator (business tier): one object encapsulates JNDI lookup and creation and caches initial contexts and home/factory objects.
